::: {#exm-conservative-interval}
#### A conservative interval for a binomial proportion

Let $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ with $n = 20$,
and let $\cintf{X}$ be the Clopper-Pearson 95% interval
returned by `binom.test()`.
Its [coverage probability](#def-coverage-probability) at each $p$ is the sum of the binomial
[probabilities](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability)
of the values $x$ of $X$ for which $\cintf{x}$ contains $p$:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
n <- 20
cp <- t(sapply(0:n, function(x) binom.test(x, n)$conf.int))
coverage <- function(p) {
  sum(dbinom(0:n, n, p)[cp[, 1] <= p & p <= cp[, 2]])
}
p_grid <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
cover <- sapply(p_grid, coverage)
range(cover)
```

The smallest coverage probability on this grid is `r sprintf("%.3f", min(cover))`,
and the largest is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(cover))`.
The grid is coarse and the coverage probability jumps at the interval endpoints,
so the smallest grid value is only an [upper bound](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets.html#def-bound) for the
[confidence coefficient](#def-confidence-coefficient).
The Clopper-Pearson interval is built to have coverage probability at least 0.95
at every $p$,
and here it is above 0.95 at
`r if (all(cover > 0.95)) "all" else paste(sum(cover > 0.95), "of the")`
`r length(p_grid)` grid values of $p$,
so it is [conservative](#def-conservative-confidence-interval).
:::
